note: Model answers are written for this tool. Mark schemes accept alternative wording, but the key words must appear. Refused wordings come from the mark schemes' 'not / ignore' notes.

items.model: The resultant force on an object is directly proportional to (or equal to) the rate of change of its momentum, and acts in the same direction.

refused.why: F = ma is a special case for constant mass, not the law.
Must be 'rate of change'.

items.model: An object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it.

refused.why: Velocity, not speed: direction matters.

items.model: When two objects interact, each exerts a force on the other that is equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and of the same type.

refused.why: Vague; say what the forces are and that they act on different objects.
The pair always acts on different objects.

items.model: The total momentum of a system remains constant, provided no external (resultant) force acts on it.
A collision in which kinetic energy is conserved (momentum is conserved as in every collision).

refused.why: Total energy is conserved in every collision; it must be kinetic energy.

items.model: A collision in which kinetic energy is not conserved; momentum and total energy still are.

refused.why: Total energy is always conserved; say kinetic energy.

items.model: The product of a force and the time for which it acts; it equals the change in momentum (the area under a force–time graph).
For an object in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same point.
The force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.

refused.why: The distance must be perpendicular.

items.model: A pair of equal and opposite parallel forces whose lines of action do not coincide; it produces rotation but no resultant force.
The resultant force is zero in every direction and the resultant moment about any point is zero.

refused.why: Too vague: say the resultant force and resultant moment are zero.

items.model: The point at which the entire weight of an object appears (can be taken) to act.

refused.why: Gravity is not a force name here; say weight.
Mass is not a force; say weight.

items.model: The maximum, constant velocity reached when the drag equals the weight (minus any upthrust), so the resultant force and acceleration are zero.

refused.why: Too vague; say the resultant force is zero.
Too vague on its own.

items.model: The upward force on an object in a fluid, equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.

refused.why: Only 'weight' of fluid displaced is accepted.
Only 'weight' of fluid displaced is accepted.

items.model: Mass per unit volume.
The normal (perpendicular) force per unit area.
The force multiplied by the distance moved in the direction of the force.
The rate of doing work, or energy transferred per unit time.
Useful output energy (or power) divided by total input energy (or power), often as a percentage.
The extension of an object is directly proportional to the force applied, provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.
Deformation in which the material returns to its original shape and size when the force is removed.
Permanent deformation: the material does not return to its original shape when the force is removed.
The maximum tensile stress a material can withstand before it breaks.

refused.why: It is a stress (force per area), not a force.

items.model: Tensile stress divided by tensile strain, for a material obeying Hooke's law (the gradient of the linear part of a stress–strain graph).
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, for example velocity, force or displacement.

refused.why: Speed is a scalar; the example must be a vector.

items.model: The rate of change of velocity.

refused.why: Velocity, not speed.

items.model: The distance moved in a specified direction from a fixed point.
The sum of the thinking distance and the braking distance.

refused.why: Must include both parts.

items.model: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value; precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other (small spread).

refused.why: That is resolution, not accuracy.

items.model: A systematic error shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction (e.g. a zero error); random errors scatter readings unpredictably about the true value and are reduced by repeating and averaging.

refused.why: Too vague; name the specific error.

items.model: The rate of flow of charge.

refused.why: Current is rate of flow of charge (carriers need not be electrons).

items.model: The charge that passes a point when a current of one ampere flows for one second.
The energy transferred from electrical energy to other forms per unit charge.
The energy transferred from other forms (e.g. chemical) into electrical energy per unit charge.
One joule per coulomb: the p.d. when one joule of energy is transferred per coulomb of charge.
Resistance is the p.d. across a component divided by the current through it; one ohm is one volt per ampere.
The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the p.d. across it, provided physical conditions such as temperature remain constant.
A property of a material equal to RA/L: the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross-sectional area.

refused.why: Resistance depends on dimensions; resistivity does not.

items.model: The sum of the currents entering a junction equals the sum of the currents leaving it (conservation of charge).
Around any closed loop, the sum of the e.m.f.s equals the sum of the p.d.s (conservation of energy).
Internal resistance is the resistance of the source itself; lost volts are the p.d. across it (Ir), equal to the e.m.f. minus the terminal p.d.
The number of free charge carriers per unit volume of the material.

refused.why: All atoms contain electrons; it must be free charge carriers.

items.model: The average velocity of the charge carriers along the conductor.
An oscillation that travels through a medium (or space), transferring energy from one place to another without transferring matter.
Wavelength: the minimum distance between two points oscillating in phase. Amplitude: the maximum displacement from equilibrium. Frequency: the number of oscillations per unit time.

refused.why: Acceptable only as 'two adjacent peaks'; points in phase is safer.

items.model: The difference in phase, in degrees or radians, between two points on a wave or between two waves.

refused.why: Needs a comparison between two points or waves.

items.model: In a transverse wave the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer; in a longitudinal wave they are parallel to it.

refused.why: Particles oscillate or vibrate; 'move' is refused.

items.model: A transverse wave whose oscillations are confined to one plane only, perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.

refused.why: Say oscillations in one plane.

items.model: When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement equals the sum of the individual displacements.

refused.why: It is about displacements at an instant, not amplitudes.

items.model: Two waves are coherent if they have a constant phase difference (and so the same frequency).

refused.why: 'Same' is refused; it must be constant.
Coherent waves need not be in phase.
Ignored: coherence means a constant phase difference.

items.model: The difference in the distances travelled by two waves from their sources to a point, usually expressed in wavelengths.

refused.why: Path difference is a length (in m or λ), not cycles or an angle.

items.model: The superposition of coherent waves, producing a pattern of maxima (constructive) and minima (destructive).

refused.why: Say superposition.
Say superposition of coherent waves.

items.model: Constructive: waves arrive in phase (path difference nλ), giving maximum amplitude. Destructive: waves arrive in antiphase (path difference (n + ½)λ), giving minimum amplitude.
The spreading out of waves as they pass through a gap or around an obstacle.

refused.why: 'Spreading' is the expected term.

items.model: A wave formed by the superposition of two progressive waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions; it has nodes (zero amplitude) and antinodes (maximum amplitude) and no net energy transfer.
A node is a point of zero amplitude; an antinode is a point of maximum amplitude.
The speed of light in a vacuum divided by the speed of light in the material.

refused.why: It must be the speed in a vacuum.

items.model: The angle of incidence (in the denser medium) for which the angle of refraction is 90°.

refused.t: minimum angle for total internal reflection
refused.why: Ignored as insufficient; define it by the 90° refraction angle.

items.model: A quantum (discrete packet) of electromagnetic energy, with energy E = hf.
The energy gained by an electron when it is accelerated through a potential difference of one volt (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J).
The emission of electrons from a metal surface when electromagnetic radiation above the threshold frequency falls on it.
The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of a metal.

refused.why: Restating the effect doesn't define it.

items.model: The minimum frequency of electromagnetic radiation that will release electrons from the surface of a metal.

refused.why: Say electromagnetic radiation or photons, not just 'wave'.

items.model: The maximum kinetic energy of an emitted photoelectron; hf is the energy of one photon and φ the work function.

refused.why: Describes the symbols; say hf is the energy of a photon.

items.model: The wavelength associated with a moving particle, equal to the Planck constant divided by its momentum (λ = h/p).

refused.why: Electrons behave as waves; they do not become waves.
